World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: China quietly turns off supply of world's most used industrial chemical
World.content:
China has moved to protect its supply of the world's most used industrial chemical, with ramifications for everything from food production to fashion and mobile phones.

Sulphuric acid is a crucial ingredient in the manufacture of batteries, clothing and phosphate fertilisers, and is also used to treat drinking water, purify petroleum, and produce some metals and computer chips.

China is a key exporter, but it relies on imported sulphur — itself a by-product of oil refining and smelting — to make it.

In 2025, about half of the global sulphur supply came from the Middle East.

With trade disrupted, Beijing has banned exports of sulphuric acid to shore up its domestic supply.

It means Australian manufacturers are facing a difficult choice — either stock up on the highly corrosive and combustible chemical, or go without their key ingredient.

The key ingredient's key ingredient

In Geelong in south-western Victoria, textile manufacturer LoomTex is trying to keep its heritage of weaving, dying and milling alive through sustainable fabrics.

Chief executive Samantha Van Zyl said sulphuric acid was one of several chemicals relied on in research and development.

Samantha Van Zyl says sulphuric acid is a necessary ingredient in making textiles. (Supplied: Loomtex)

"It's critical as an auxiliary step in the lab … for fibre innovation," she said.

The supply disruption puts the company in a difficult position.

Ms Van Zyl said they were left with the choice to either order more sulphuric acid than normal, which puts them above the threshold for storing dangerous goods, or not have enough supply.

"Increasing to the dangerous goods limit actually means that we're changing the shape of our business," she said.

"We'd have to bring in WorkSafe Victoria; the fire hazards and safety risks on site as a chemical risk profile completely change.

"It's not something that can be done overnight."

Samantha Van Zyl says LoomTex is struggling to source three types of acid, including sulphuric. (Supplied: Kate Ballis)

Ms Van Zyl said that without the acids, production would suffer, and she could lose customers to overseas manufacturers.

"That's a vulnerability and a risk I don't think that we would look to take at this point in time," she said.

LoomTex relies on multiple types of acid in its production process. (Supplied: Stu Ross/Milk Video)

Sulphuric acid is made two ways; either using sulphur or as a by-product of metal smelting.

Head of sulphur and sulphuric acid research at Argus Consulting Services, Meena Chauhan, said the acid was produced worldwide, but China was the lead exporter.

"Last year, they exported close to 5 million tonnes for the first time," she said.

" It's a substantial volume in that global trade flow. "

China relies on importing sulphur, a by-product from oil refining and gas processing, to make sulphuric acid.

In 2025, about 73 million tonnes of sulphur was produced globally.

"We estimated that Middle Eastern trade represented about 50 per cent of global trade flows," Ms Chauhan said.

The Middle East represents more than half of the global sulphur trade. (Reuters)

She said the effect of the Iran war on supply was twofold: the closed Strait of Hormuz stopped vessels carrying it, and damage was caused to refineries and processors in the region that produced it.

"Some sites are being taken offline because of damage; in other cases because of precautionary measures," she said.

She said China's ban on exporting sulphuric acid, which came into effect on May 1, was an attempt to protect their "downstream industries" from disruption.

Attention is turning to other sulphur-exporting countries like Canada for an alternative supply, but Ms Chauhan said there were issues with logistics and volume.

Australia produces some sulphuric acid for its domestic market from metal smelting in Queensland, but not at the grade Ms Van Zyl's textile lab requires.

But local supplies may help the leading end user of both sulphur and sulphuric acid — the fertiliser industry.

Building block of food security

North West Phosphate mines phosphate rock and concentrate in Queensland, which is used by fertiliser manufacturers throughout South-East Asia.

Chairman John Cotter said sulphuric acid was a critical element for his customers.

John Cotter says changes in the fertiliser trade might affect his business. (ABC North West Qld: Emily Dobson)

"Most of those producers use sulphur mixed with water to create sulphuric acid mixed in with phosphate rock," he said.

"That gives you the basic ingredients for all of the fertiliser blends that you find in the shops."

So far, his business had not been impacted, but Mr Cotter expected it to happen soon.

"For suppliers like us, we're worried that if [customers] can't get the other basic ingredient to manufacture, then we might have to divert to other markets," he said.

"These are the sort of structural changes in the trading market of commodities globally that we're seeing as a result of the conflict."

Ms Chauhan said Mr Cotter's fears were warranted.

Versatility and variability

Sulphuric acid did not become the world's most widely used industrial chemical based on its versatility alone.

As the by-product of a by-product, historically it has also been pretty cheap.

But with demand for both chemicals also coming from the metal industry, which can absorb higher prices, Ms Chauhan said fertiliser production could not compete.

"In some markets, South Africa, we've seen [reduced production]," she said.

" We've seen in North Africa as well, a key fertiliser producer announcing that they're going to have a reduction in their output of fertilisers. "

Once the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, Ms Chauhan said shipments of oil and gas would likely be prioritised over sulphur, potentially dragging out shortages for years.

Additionally, she said sulphur producers had reported it could be years before damaged facilities were back to pre-war capacity.

Prior to the war, the oil and gas industry had been expanding in the Middle East, which would also have increased production, but Ms Chauhan said those projects were also now on hold.

"The war is impacting revenues, impacting the timelines for these projects that will now likely end up with delays through until next year, potentially even beyond next year," she said.

Back in the Geelong textile warehouse, Samantha Van Zyl is carrying on, despite the odds.

"It is a bit stacked up [against you]," she said.

"But you just wake up, put a smile on your face and pull up your sleeves and get into it," she said.

"It's all we can do, really."

LoomTex uses sulphuric acid in its dye process. (Supplied: Stu Ross/Milk Video)

World.title: Push to make rental properties ready for portable power future
World.content:
At Robin Sands's rental property, he only has to buy about half his electricity from the grid.

Despite not owning the unit in Wollongong, he has done just about everything possible to lower his energy bills.

With his landlord's permission, he has mounted two portable solar panels on his roof to power his kitchen appliances during the day, as well as charge two lithium batteries that take over when the sun sets.

"The two panels on a good sunny day can get up to 4 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of charging, but I regularly need about 2kWh a day to run those appliances and my general consumption is about 6kWh a day," he said.

Two solar panels deliver enough power to run Robin Sands's kitchen appliances during the day and charge two batteries. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

" It doesn't fully pay for everything, but it's been really worth the effort to reduce my bills significantly. "

Mr Sands cooks on a $180 portable induction cooktop, has installed a free hot water heat pump as part of a government scheme, and can control his LED lighting from his phone.

When he does buy electricity from the grid, he purchases green power.

Robin Sands says some small adjustments to his property have had a big impact on his power bill. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Campaign for renters to plug in

Rental homes are significantly less energy efficient than owner-occupied homes, with the disparity particularly acute in low-income and regional areas.

The NSW government is exploring minimum energy efficiency standards for rental properties, arguing even simple measures like insulation could slash energy bills by up to $750 a year.

Electrification advocacy group Rewiring Australia is preparing a submission to the state government pushing for electric appliances to replace gas fittings at the end of their life.

The organisation has also written a discussion paper calling for portable energy set-ups like "balcony solar" systems to be allowed to power household appliances in rentals.

Francis Vierboom says the uptake of electric vehicles will see residents start using them to power their homes. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

They also want a dedicated plug to allow higher-power, bi-directional charging that would allow tenants to plug in their own batteries, such as an electric vehicle battery, to supply power to the home.

"You can power a typical house off a car battery for five days, and this technology will allow you to do that," Rewiring Australia chief executive Francis Vierboom said.

"We're all going to start using cars that have a gigantic battery in them, double the size of even the big home batteries people are installing now.

"Connecting your car at a scale that can run your house can take a big bite out of your energy bills and if we get that set-up right early, we can make sure renters don't miss out on the next wave of technology."

Preparing for portable power

Mr Vierboom said current rules meant a vehicle-to-grid power box had to be hardwired into a house, requiring landlord approval, and could not be taken when the tenant moved out.

Rewiring Australia hopes renters will be able to install vehicle-to-grid boxes like this one. (Supplied: Jai Nankivell)

A specific plug could change that.

"If we design a safe, standard plug we'd expect to see installed in garages, to put in this [vehicle to grid] equipment that's safe for this power to connect into your house, we might see renters use that car battery," Mr Vierboom said.

" There's an opportunity now to look at how this equipment can be moved around so renters can get it and make their car part of the power system. "

Francis Vierboom says the three hours of free power will be particularly useful for renters. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Taking advantage of free power

On July 1 this year, people in NSW with a smart meter will be able to opt in to access three hours of free daytime electricity (capped at 25kWh) as part of the Solar Sharer Offer.

It is a federal government initiative designed to soak up excess solar power and encourage people to use appliances like washing machines and dryers during times of abundant renewable energy.

Robin Sands has used his technical knowledge to fit his garage out with energy efficiencies. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Mr Vierboom said it could benefit renters with a portable battery of any kind.

"You could charge your car quickly during the day for three hours and then power your house [from it] through peak evening hours," he said.

"It's an interesting alternative to getting solar and batteries installed."

World.title: Disabled Australians on love, lust and the right to intimacy
World.content:
It's a stormy February night in Adelaide, and Jacqueline Tedmanson is at the hospital with her partner Jackson, waiting to meet their first baby.

Despite having a disability, Jacqueline isn't nervous about the birth. She's just excited to be having a child, and the couple only hope the child "is funny" rather than "healthy".

As a queer disabled person, burlesque gives Jacqueline Tedmanson, aka Diana Divine, a rare space to be sexy and powerful, without feeling infantilised or fetishised. (Compass: Johanis Lyons-Reid)

Jacqueline has Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS), an incurable and frequently painful condition that causes joints to be overly flexible and prone to dislocation.

EDS is genetic, and Jacqueline knows that her son could have inherited it. But she's not worried about it because she knows how to help him manage the condition.

"There are people I know who, it barely affects them … And then there are people like me who are relying on mobility aids daily," Jacqueline said.

"I think, if at least, if he has this genetic disability, I am going to be able to support him because I've been through it myself."

Like most people with EDS, Jacqueline was diagnosed in adulthood after years of living with chronic pain and injury.

She says she will be aware if her son shows signs of the condition and will be able to advocate for him where her own parents couldn't.

Comedian Madeleine Stewart explores these stories of disability love, sex and parenting with Compass ABC TV. She talks to the disabled community across Australia to find out what the big deal is with disabled sex.

"I think we need to remind people that … disabled folk … not only can we fall in love and have sex, but we can also have children," Madeleine said.

When Debra Keenahan found out she was pregnant, she was hoping the baby would share her disability.

Debra has achondroplasia, also known as Dwarfism.

Dwarfism is a genetic condition that occurs in about 40,000 children, and most are born to average height parents.

Having Dwarfism herself and knowing that the father was of average height, Debra knew it was likely her child would also have achondroplasia.

Debra Keenahan (right) met her husband, Robert Brindley, on a photo shoot in 2014. (Compass: Morgan Timms)

"I just had it in my head it would be easier to parent a child that was my own gender … And it would be easier to, if the child was short-statured," Debra said.

"Of course, if she'd have been a boy, I would have been perfectly happy. [But] in my family, all my nephews are massive.

" And I thought, could you imagine me, a single parent, four-foot-one, trying to parent an obnoxious six-foot teenager? "

Debra felt relieved when she found that her daughter, Sarah, had achondroplasia too.

Raising the child as a single parent had its challenges, but Debra never felt she was less equipped to handle it because of her disability.

She recalls some criticism from others when she would let Sarah struggle with navigating climbing furniture because she knew it was something her daughter would have to learn to do.

Jacqueline hasn't been criticised for her choice to have a child, but when people see her with her son while using a walker, they make assumptions about their relationship.

" Often Jackson will be carrying [the baby] if I'm using a walker, and I do sometimes feel like I am assumed to not be the parent, I'm just kind of with him and his son, maybe not even in a romantic way. "

The systemic barriers no-one wants to talk about

People with disabilities make up about 21 per cent of the Australian population and an even larger percentage will develop a disability with age, the ABS reported in 2022.

Despite the numbers, having safe sex or raising a family are more difficult for people with disabilities than for the able-bodied and neurotypical population.

People with disabilities are often victims of sexual assault and domestic violence, and on occasion, forced sterilisation is used to prevent childbirth.

Madeleine Stewart says: "People with disability should be given room and support to explore their sexuality." (Supplied)

The Australian Human Rights Commission found overwhelmingly that young women with intellectual disability were subjected to forced sterilisation and not always in accordance with the law.

In Queensland legislation, a person with a cognitive disability, ranging from an intellectual disability to dementia to autism, is deemed incapable of consenting to sex, and their partners can be arrested for sexual abuse if they break that law.

For some people with disabilities, their only option for intimate contact is to engage sex workers, but it's an expensive option, used by few, and no longer supported by the NDIS after a change to legislation in October 2024 to make the Scheme "more sustainable".

Kyle Montgomery found the sudden lack of intimacy was one of the hardest parts of living with an acquired disability.

Seven years ago, Kyle's neck was broken in a wrestling match with a friend, and it left him paralysed below the chest.

Like many men his age, Kyle Montgomery still has a strong interest in sex. (Compass: Nisa East)

Kyle has had to get used to most of his contact coming from support workers and learn to navigate his own body again.

"That is definitely a weird area when it comes to support workers, because you're very close and intimate with people," Kyle said.

"I am naked all the time in the mornings, obviously. So, things like massage and stretching, I'm nude.

"They're helping me go to the toilet, showering me, washing my body, things like that … So there is a lot of intimate touch.

"I don't think it's very uncommon for people who have support workers and maybe not dating, and they're alone to feel an attraction to their support worker."

This is what sex therapist Patrick Rory-John calls "calcification" of sexuality.

"What can happen with people with disability is through the calcification of sexuality and its repression … it becomes an impulse because it's a need that's not being met," Patrick said.

" When a person with disability is experiencing touch during basic hygiene and care, they can misconstrue that touch as being sensual or sexual, and what is a desire becomes a compulsion. "

Rediscovering intimacy after an acquired disability

A lack of intimacy inspired Kyle to start dating again, but he was nervous about how the first experience would work, so his friend encouraged him to start with sex workers.

"Erections started happening, and I was like, 'Oh, it still works. Cool'," Kyle said.

"I didn't really feel like I had the confidence to go dating and have a sex life because I don't obviously know about my body.

" I really didn't want to navigate those conversations with someone that's inexperienced and could be very insensitive, where I thought, this is a professional job. "

He spent a year in hospital, coming off a ventilator and getting the use of his arms back, but Kyle said discussions of having a sex life afterwards were very clinical.

"I ended up speaking to a lot of doctors about it, but they just told me about drugs and devices that I could use.

"It wasn't just about sex, which it should have been, and sexual health … It was so clinical."

Kyle is now in a monogamous relationship, and they are considering going permanent and starting a family.

Kyle is concerned about trying for children because his disability means they will likely need to use IVF, which is not only expensive but also another clinical experience.

Loading...

Disabled, intimate and starting families — the stories we don't tell

Madeleine felt it was important to tell these stories of parenting after the NDIS change of legislation prevented access to sex workers and sexual aids.

"People with disability should be given room and support to explore their sexuality. It can be a really positive experience," Madeleine said

"And we can also be amazing partners and parents as well."

Jacqueline is looking forward to raising a child and helping him learn about the world.

"I'm really excited to be a parent and to kind of help navigate the world with a little person," she said.

" I do think, being queer and disabled, I kind of have a lot of understanding of how tough the world can be, but also how nice it can be with community and with people who really love and support you. "

Watch From Intimate Access on Compass tonight at 6:30pm on ABC TV or stream now on iview.

World.title: 'You're malnourished; you are overtrained': Olympic gymnast's warning
World.content:
Alexandra Kiroi-Bogatyreva spent years sacrificing her health for a shot at making the Olympics.

"I was so driven that injuries didn't stop me," the 24-year-old told ABC Sport.

"I really wanted to achieve my goals, show the world what I'm capable of and give back to my family."

The rhythmic gymnast competed in the 2024 Paris Olympics and medalled at the 2018 and 2022 Commonwealth Games.

She retired at 22 years old, noting that most athletes typically leave the sport between 17 and 21.

"The sport demands significant physical commitment, as well as considerable psychological resilience," she said.

Kiroi-Bogatyreva trained up to 10 hours a day, six days a week, but it was often without the proper nutrition.

"It's very hard for a gymnast [being an] aesthetic sport, to be told you should eat more carbs when you're raised in the culture of being thin is better," Kiroi-Bogatyreva said.

It meant her body wasn't functioning the way it should have been.

Kiroi-Bogatyreva didn't get her first period until she was 19. At that age, most women have had theirs for about seven years.

Doctors told Kiroi-Bogatyreva that her body didn't have enough energy to have a period. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling)

After that, it would only come once a year, when she had a two-week break from gymnastics.

"No one really questioned why, or if it's okay for that to be happening," she said.

It wasn't until years later that doctors explained what was going on.

"I was [told] 'you're malnourished, you are over trained and your body just doesn't have the energy to even have a period," she said.

"Before that, I never really linked it with my food intake or how many hours I trained at the gym."

It's this normalisation of menstrual dysfunction that athletes like Kiroi-Bogatyreva want to see changed.

They also want more knowledge about how to approach the menstrual cycle, and to raise awareness about the serious consequences if overlooked.

Kiroi-Bogatyreva wants coaches to have more awareness of women's health. (ABC Sport: Patrick Stone)

Missing periods seen as sign of 'fitness'

Getting your period late, or being irregular, isn't unusual among elite athletes.

In partnership with Deakin University, ABC Sport surveyed 152 women and gender diverse athletes across 47 sports.

Seventy-five per cent of respondents said they experienced menstrual irregularities as an athlete.

The same number said menstrual cycles weren't taken into consideration when developing their training programs.

Professional ironwoman Harriet Brown said she didn't remember anyone asking about her menstrual cycle over the course of her 15-year career.

"Back then it was seen as you are really fit if you didn't have your period," the 35-year-old told ABC Sport.

Harriet Brown says when she was competing, not having your period was seen as a good thing. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

And Kiroi-Bogatyreva was led to believe just that.

"It was just well-known that if you're an athlete you get your period later," she said.

Elite sportswomen have shared their stories, and these are the hard truths Low pay, discrimination, disordered eating, sexism and online abuse are just a few of the prevalent issues ABC's Elite Athletes in Women's Sport Survey has revealed.

"There was just so much lack of education that we are really starting to realise can be really helpful," Brown said.

"These are the topics that I think would have made a really big difference to so many female athletes, including myself."

Several athletes told us that their menstrual irregularities and symptoms were dismissed or ignored by coaching staff.

One survey respondent wrote:

"I was told to go to training anyway, when my chronic illness (PMOS, formerly PCOS) left me bedridden for a few days during my period each month, to 'practice what it would be like if it happened in competition'. No opportunity for reasonable adjustments. There was never a question of whether I could train, or care for whether I should."

Another said:

"There is no consideration of support for athletes on their period, how to manage pain or recovery. There's also no acknowledgement or tailoring of training. Sometimes my pain is so bad I can barely walk yet I push through a training session, how is this helpful?"

Pill use could be masking health problems

To help with managing the menstrual cycle, some athletes are put on the contraceptive pill, including many survey respondents.

Although using the pill can help some people, it can also hide more serious issues.

"It can be pretty impactful as an athlete because what it can be masking is RED-S [relative energy deficiency] in sport," Brown, who is also an exercise physiologist, said.

RED-S happens when you use up more calories than you take in. You might feel tired, miss periods, or get colds or infections.

You're more likely to get hurt because your body will take longer to recover after exercise, and down the track there's a risk of fertility problems, bone weakness and osteoporosis.

"The body starts to slow down, down-regulate some systems and one of those systems that potentially starts to go is the menstrual cycle, or hormones, and so an athlete will no longer have a period," Brown said.

Brown now focuses on giving female athletes the information she wishes she had while competing. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Brown didn't get her first period until 16. She doesn't know exactly why but cites RED-S as a potential factor.

She went on the pill for about nine years while competing and struggled with knowing how much she needed to fuel.

"I was significantly under-eating because I had no idea how much an athlete training 15 times a week needed to eat," Brown said.

"I have no idea if I had a healthy period throughout my career or not.

"When I went off [the pill], I had a much better understanding around nutrition, I was fuelling enough, so I did get a healthy period after that."

Lack of menstrual management can have long-term health impacts

Ignoring menstrual irregularities can have serious long-term health implications.

Ro Nogueira is an anatomist at Bond University and an exercise physiologist, and said hormones, particularly oestrogen, played a crucial role in bone health.

Ro Nogueira is an assistant professor in the Faculty of Health Sciences and Medicine at Bond University. (Supplied: Bond University)

"You have to consider that low energy availability highly influences bone health," she said.

"If you're not supplying your body with enough nutrients, that's when hormonal levels will be at risk.

"As a result, the bone mineral density of athletes will be reduced, and they will be much more prone to become osteoporotic in the future."

Kiroi-Bogatyreva suffered multiple bone fractures throughout her career.

"I've had major competitions where I competed with stress fractures in both feet at the same time," she said.

"I broke a finger the day before a competition. Three months later it was still sore and I went to get an X-ray, and it was like, 'Oh, it's broken'.

"The whole time I was training with a broken finger. I just ignored any pain I had."

Kiroi-Bogatyreva is now coaching the next generation of rhythmic gymnasts. (ABC Sport: Patrick Stone)

Fertility can also be an issue. If you don't have a healthy menstrual cycle, you may not be ovulating and therefore are unable to conceive.

Brown retired from racing two years ago and had a baby late last year.

Although falling pregnant wasn't the only reason she decided to stop racing, it was a contributing factor.

"I knew it would be really difficult to fall pregnant whilst I was training 15, 16 times a week," Brown said.

"My body was not in a great state for facilitating carrying a baby with the energy output that I was having."

Harriet Brown had baby Olive in December after retiring from professional sport. (Instagram: @zizisun)

Clubs, athletes trying to bridge the education gap

Eighty-five cent of the ABC and Deakin University survey respondents don't think there's enough education about women's health for athletes, coaches and support staff.

Although that's a big number, changes have been made across some sporting codes in recent years.

AFLW teams like the GWS Giants have been working with a sports exercise and pelvic health physiotherapist. The Western Bulldogs and Super League teams have tailored training around the menstrual cycle, and some Super Netball players are being offered free fertility checks.

Other codes like NRLW, rugby, soccer and tennis have also opted into women's health education, while the Australian Insititue of Sport's Female Performance and Health Initiative has information online.

Brown and fellow ironwoman Lizzie Welborn have created an educational platform called KaMana, where they speak about menstrual health, body image, nutrition and performance mindset to athletes, coaches and support staff from community level to elite.

Loading Instagram content

"[It's] all of the education we wish we had when we were younger athletes," Brown said.

"Talking about these things can be so empowering, and not just help athletes at the elite level but also help with participation in sport."

Participation is a key concern when it comes to adolescent girls, with drop-out linked to the menstrual cycle.

Brown and Welborn speak to athletes about menstrual health, body image, nutrition and performance mindset. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Michaela Hardy used to swim at a national level and had issues navigating her period in the pool.

"In the middle of a session, I was on my period, I was cramping, I was quite exhausted and tired," Hardy told ABC Sport.

"My coach stopped me, told me to hop out of the pool and said that I wasn't training hard enough.

"That was the moment I realised there's no safe way for me to say, 'Hey, I'm on my period, this is where I'm at'."

She doesn't want others to face the same challenges she did, so she's created an app aiming for change where athletes can log their cycle, symptoms, mood and energy levels, then choose exactly what information is shared with their coach.

Michaela Hardy created an app where athletes can share information about their cycle, symptoms, mood and energy levels. (Supplied: Bond University)

The goal is to support cycle-aware training, reduce injury risk, and remove the stigma around periods in sport.

"What I'd love my coaches to have known, was just knowing about the four phases [of the menstrual cycle] and how they can best train their athletes around that," Hardy said.

Hardy hopes her app will also help keep girls in sport during their teenage years.

"My long-term vision is that every female athlete within Australia is empowered to communicate with their coach where they're at in their menstrual cycle, and doesn't feel their menstrual cycle is taboo, but actually can help performance and overall wellbeing," she said.

ABC Women's Sport Survey: Results summary Here is a summary of the results from ABC Sport's inaugural Elite Athletes in Australian Women's Sport Survey, in partnership with Deakin University.

Brown believes coaches have a big part to play in helping women feel comfortable to speak up about their menstrual cycles.

"It's high-performance sport, it's physiology, it shouldn't just be a taboo topic anymore," she said.

As a coach now herself, Kiroi-Bogatyreva wants to be there for her students, on and off the mat.

"Throughout my career, I experienced both exceptional coaching and situations that taught me what I would do differently," she said.

"Those experiences have shaped the coach I strive to be: someone who supports athletes holistically, develops them both as individuals and performers, and provides a consistent, trusted presence throughout their journey.

"I spent 10 hours a day with [my] coach, and same with these gymnasts we coach now.

"So, I think if coaches start being more aware of the issues around food and overtraining, they can implement strategies to stop it, [and] I think the culture will shift."

This story is part of the ABC Elite Athletes in Australian Women's Sport Survey.

World.title: Why some Australian homebuyers are turning to Islamic financing
World.content:
When Wildan Al Hazmi decided to buy an investment property several years ago he did not even consider a conventional loan.

Instead, he opted for a niche option that caters to a growing segment of Australia's population.

Mr Al Hazmi, a father of two in Melbourne, said he took out Islamic financing because of his Muslim faith.

"The reason for using Islamic financing is the peace of mind that comes from complying with Islamic principles such as avoiding riba (interest) and sourced from halal products," he said.

Borrowers do not need be Muslim to access Islamic financing, but in Australia it is rarely the cheaper option.

So how does Islamic financing actually work? How is it different from traditional loans? And if it is not cheaper why do people choose it?

Why some people are choosing this option

Euis Amalia, the professor of Islamic economics at Universitas Islam Negeri (UIN) Syarif Hidayatullah Jakarta, said Islamic transactions prohibited three things: riba (interest), gharar (speculative transaction), and maisyir (gambling activity).

She said interest was considered "unjust and exploitative" because it created an imbalance between capital owners and borrowers, placing the most risk on the borrowers.

Professor Amalia said, generally speaking, conventional banking primarily focused on profit generation while the Islamic economics system also "prioritises human and environmental welfare".

Professor Euis Amalia said a popular Islamic financing structure was "Murabaha" or "risk sharing". (Supplied)

She said all financial transactions involved must be halal, meaning they cannot be linked to prohibited activities that bring more harm than good for society or the environment.

This means those institutions are forbidden from investing in certain industries including gambling, alcohol and pornography.

In the context of mortgages, transactions in Islamic finance must be based on a clear deal between the buyer and the seller, Professor Amalia said.

"Islamic finance is governed by ethical principles like prohibiting exploitation and speculation, as well as income derived from such activities," she said.

How does it work?

Professor Amalia said one popular Islamic financing structure was "Murabaha" or "risk sharing" where an Islamic finance service buys an asset — such as a house — and resells it to a buyer with a marked-up profit.

The "profit rate" is benchmarked to market interest rates.

Similar to conventional banking, Islamic financing includes fixed rate and variable rate schemes.

If the mark-up is fixed, any decisions by the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise the cash rate would not affect the repayments once the contract is signed.

The buyer would pay the financier in fixed instalments over an agreed duration, up to a decade, similar to the idea of a fixed rate in conventional banking.

The moral foundations of Islamic banking Islam is not the only religious tradition to have raised serious concerns about the ethics of interest, but Muslims have continued to debate the issue with vigour.

According to MCCA Islamic Finance and Investments, a provider of Islamic financing, while the Reserve Bank of Australia "does not directly regulate Islamic finance products, its policies influence the overall economic conditions in which these products are offered."

"For instance, changes in the cash rate can affect the cost of borrowing for Islamic finance contracts," its website said.

While a Murabaha agreement and a fixed-term loan can look similar, experts argue they are built on different structures.

Salaam is a Sydney-based company that provides home financing in compliance with Islamic principles.

"Interest is charged on lending money, while the profit rate is the agreed return from a sales contract under a real asset," said Mas Johan Harris, the head of investment and product at Salaam.

Mas Johan Harris said the limited Islamic finance market in Australia had affected its affordability. (Supplied)

Another common Islamic financing structure is Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek or the "shared ownership model".

This is a structure in which the Islamic financier and the home owner jointly purchase the property, and the home owner then pays monthly rent, plus a profit margin, to the financier for the share they own.

Eventually the property is paid off and the homebuyer owns the property outright, similar to shared equity schemes.

This is the structure that Mr Al Hazmi used when he bought his two-bedroom investment property in Thuringowa, in Central Queensland.

Mr Al Hazmi bought this house in 2024. (Supplied)

He bought the house for $486,500 in 2023 and took out a 30-year variable rate instalment plan.

He pays around $2,500 every month including a "profit rate".

At the end of the 30 years, Mr Al Hazmi would have paid about $1 million for the property.

Since Australian property and tax laws are designed around conventional mortgages, Islamic finance providers may offer different legal structures to avoid extra costs like double stamp duty.

For example, Mr Al Hazmi's name is on the title of his investment property, but he has a separate contract with his Islamic finance institution detailing the shared ownership arrangement.

Can it work out cheaper than a conventional loan?

Irwan Anto, an independent broker in Melbourne, said the cost of Islamic finance services in Australia is usually a bit more expensive than the conventional banks due to several factors.

Irwan Anto said only a small number of his clients chose Islamic financing for their mortgage. (Supplied)

"One of the reasons is because they have to pay the Islamic legal team [to arrange the documentation]," he said.

Mr Harris, from Salaam, said this included Islamic-compliant certification issued annually to ensure the product complied with Islamic law.

Melike and Ibrahim don't pay interest. Here's how and why Australia's finance sector is tapping into the Islamic market with one of the country's biggest lenders launching a Sharia-compliant loan.

The certificates were sourced from specialist consultancy firms in Dubai and Malaysia.

While strong competition among conventional lenders made the rates more competitive, Mr Harris said the Islamic financing market was smaller in Australia.

He said this meant the cost of funding the mortgage could be higher.

However, Professor Amalia said in countries with a larger Islamic finance market, like Indonesia, the cost could be cheaper.

"For example, Sharia Bank of Indonesia can set a considerably cheaper price because they have a huge capital and transaction volume," she said.

The slightly more expensive option did not deter Mr Al Hazmi to use an Islamic financing service as he was after "peace of mind".

"The main benefit lies in prioritising values over profit, focusing on fulfilling the commandments of God rather than purely financial gain," he said.

Is this the only option for Muslim borrowers?

Loading...

According to Australian Bureau of Statistics Census data the country's Muslim population has steadily grown, rising from 476,300 in 2011 to 813,400 in 2021.

Mr Anto said within the Muslim community many still compared conventional and Islamic finance options.

"Only a small amount of my clients are choosing an Islamic finance service due to the higher overall cost," he said.

Fikrie Afiff, a Muslim man living in Melbourne, decided to take out a conventional mortgage with a variable rate in 2019.

"At that time I was looking for the lowest overall cost option," he said.

Fikrie Afiff said he would consider switching to Islamic financing in the future. (Supplied)

However, a series of cash rate rises between late 2022 and 2023 put financial pressure on his family.

Mr Afiff said he would consider switching to Islamic financing in the future if he could bear the costs.

He said when he recently consulted an Islamic scholar he was advised that he should hold off switching if the higher monthly repayments would burden the family.

"[He said] it is better to postpone it until I am ready," Mr Afiff said.

World.title: Aspiration has changed since the Howard era. This budget is finally catching up
World.content:
The word "aspirational" means something very different in contemporary Australia, compared to what it used to mean.

At the turn of the century, during the peak of the Howard era, it described Australians who wanted to put their kids into private school and university, and to build their wealth by getting an investment property or two.

John Howard and Peter Costello actively encouraged this by implementing generous tax breaks for investments, such as the 50 per cent discount on capital gains and tax-free retirement incomes from super.

Leveling the property playing field There's no doubt that taking away negative gearing on existing properties will even the playing field but they aren't a cure all.

But the wealth those measures helped to create for the baby boomers and gen Xs who took full advantage of them has come at the expense of opportunities for their children and grandchildren to do the same.

Today, aspiration means something humbler; millions of younger Australians simply aspire to own a home one day, to have some shelter.

Everybody knows the era has gone when a young family could buy a home on a single income by "working hard" and saving.

In the past few decades, as property prices have risen much faster than wages, a pillar of Australia's post-war egalitarianism (and its famous "property-owning democracy") has been destroyed, taking parts of our culture with it.

Younger Australians are furious about it. They've been screaming about it for years. And now it's finally, belatedly, impacting our national politics.

High income tax burden on workers has to be reduced

This week, Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese hammered the final nail into the coffin of the Howard-era tax breaks.

After years of both Liberal and Labor governments slowly unpicking the most generous of the superannuation rorts, Jim Chalmers has undone the capital gains tax discount that helped to supercharge Australia's property boom.

Reserve Bank research shows that, since the 1970s, there has been a gradual increase in the share of income paid to capital owners and a falling share paid to workers. (Productivity Commission, "Wealth transfers and their economic effects," Research Paper, November 2021, page 69.)

While he was at it, he also took a swing at the longstanding tax minimisation tool of trusts.

And if you read the budget papers closely enough on budget night, it was obvious that the government's housing reforms were the start of a much larger project to reform Australia's tax system.

Why Chalmers reined in the property tax lurks One of the more striking elements from the now well-entrenched program of pre-budget leaks is the lack of outrage from the population or even the opposition.

More big tax changes will be coming.

Because, as Treasury officials explained, Australia's tax system is under growing pressure from demographic and economic change.

The personal income tax burden is getting worse for workers as our population ages and the share of working-age Australians keeps shrinking.

In 1982–83, there were 6.6 working-age Australians for every Australian over the age of 65. By 2022–23, that ratio had fallen to 3.8. It is projected to fall further to 2.6 by 2062–63.

And, while the tax base of workers erodes, the government's structural spending needs are increasing, particularly on care and support services linked to an aging population.

If policy settings don't change, this story won't end well for younger workers (or Australia's social compact).

(Federal Budget 2026-27, Budget Paper No. 1, page. 138)

"A greater tax burden on salaries and wages limits the ability of younger Australians to save and accrue wealth," the budget papers warned.

"Each generation of Australians should have at least the same opportunity to build wealth and a prosperous future as the generations that came before them.

"However, today's younger Australians face weaker prospects of building wealth than earlier generations, and wealth gaps between age groups are growing," they warned.

(Federal Budget 2026-27, Budget Paper No. 1, page. 139)

Tax settings have 'exacerbated' housing affordability issues

That explains why the Albanese government wants to change the tax treatment of housing.

It wants to make it easier for young wage earners to accrue wealth by re-linking property price growth to wage growth, so that they can more easily afford to buy a home of their own.

Four charts that explain the story behind Labor's tax changes Just like it did in 2019, Labor is making an argument about wealth in Australia when it proposes negative gearing and capital gains tax changes.

It doesn't want young people to feel the need to pour their savings into the stock market and crypto to try to make enough money to afford a home because wages are for suckers in an economy ruled by asset price inflation.

In the budget, Treasury officials say the key reason why housing has become less affordable is that housing supply has not kept pace with rising demand from both home owners and investors, pushing up prices. But tax settings have also "exacerbated" affordability issues.

"These tax advantages have increased the share of housing owned by investors, at the expense of Australians looking to buy a home," they say.

AustralianSuper boss questions whether there is a real desire for more affordable housing AustralianSuper boss says housing prices unlikely to fall much, because major banks can't afford them too

So Chalmers says we need to rebalance the incentives in our tax system from income earned from assets back to income earned from labour, and his budget provides the architecture to do that.

And if his plans go through, Australia's economy will slowly adjust as people learn to pour less money into residential property and invest more money into businesses, shares, or commercial property.

Although there are some financial advisers warning that many of these investments will also be less attractive under the new tax changes.

But already, we're seeing headlines like this: 'The days of multiple properties are over': How to invest after the budget."

It's a step in the right direction, Ken Henry says

Ken Henry, a former treasury secretary who has been banging on for years about the "intergenerational inequity" in Australia's modern tax system, has applauded the budget.

Three years ago, he gave a speech to the Tax Institute that warned about many of the problems this budget is now talking about.

There is 'extraordinary intergenerational inequity' in the tax system Australian policymakers have blown the mining boom, and it will take years to turn things around, says former Treasury secretary Ken Henry.

He warned that this generation of young workers, weighed down by HECS debt, burdened with the responsibility of repaying a mountain of public debt and dealing with the costs of climate change, were finding it increasingly difficult to buy a home.

He said they were being priced out of the housing market by people who had already retired or were moving into retirement, who were sitting on tax-free capital gains in houses that were exempt from the pension assets test, and who were receiving refundable franking credits on share portfolios and a blend of publicly funded and tax-free private pensions from assets accumulated in lightly taxed self-managed superannuation funds.

"At some point, perhaps even already, the intergenerational social compact must surely fracture," he warned.

He has welcomed the budget's attempt to confront those issues.

"Finally, a budget of economic reform. It has been too long coming," he wrote in the Guardian last week. "[T]his budget doesn't fix everything. But make no mistake. Jim Chalmers' budget takes a very big step. And it is a step in the right direction. "This feels like a budget crafted with the same policy disciplines that drove the reforms of the 1980s and 1990s, reforms that set Australia up for an extended period of prosperity that was the envy of the world. On this, the treasurer should be congratulated."

It was high praise from someone who was deeply involved in the "last great reform era" in Australia.

Right now, the treasurer will take all the budget praise he can get, as large sections of the media take aim at his proposed tax changes.

World.title: Trump is painting DC's reflecting pool. Here's why people are angry
World.content:
Donald Trump has ordered a colour change at Washington DC's iconic reflecting pool.

It's the latest presidential project to generate debate — and a degree of outrage — in America's capital city.

And, as with the White House ballroom and the Paris-inspired "Arc de Trump", opponents are suing to try to stop the project.

Here are three of the big controversies surrounding the work underway at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The colour

Mr Trump says the precise shade he has requested for the pool surface is "American flag blue".

Initially, he had considered turquoise, "like in the Bahamas". But a contractor suggested the patriotic blue and "talked me into it very easily", he said.

Locals who spoke to the ABC at the site were not impressed.

"I like the idea of American flag blue, but not for the reflecting pool," said Kristine, who lives in a Virginia suburb just outside Washington DC.

" It's supposed to reflect the sky. It's not supposed to be a swimming pool. "

"'Splotchy blue' is how I would describe the colour," said Mike, a local video producer who came down to see the project after reading about it.

" I've never seen an American flag that was splotchy blue. "

Kristine (left) and Katie (right) are not happy with what is happening at the reflecting pool. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

A local non-profit, the Cultural Landscape Foundation, has filed a lawsuit to halt work, arguing proper processes were not followed.

The group says the pool's dark basin, a "signature feature" since it opened in 1924, was designed that way to create "the illusion of greater depth and a more profound reflection".

Mr Trump's chosen blue "is more appropriate to a resort or theme park", group president Charles Birnbaum said.

"I agree with that," local university student Katie told the ABC.

" I think the monuments and all of this stuff is about tradition and history … like, why is it bright blue? Why does it need to be bright blue? "

The project's $US1.8 million price tag has grown more than seven-fold to $US13.1 million. (Reuters: Annabelle Gordon)

According to a court document filed this week, the government believed the end result would not actually be all that bright.

"The finished coat — a very dark blue — will be low chroma, consistent with the Reflecting Pool's historic character and design," a summary of the government's position said.

A Washington court has ordered the government to file a response to the lawsuit by Monday.

The contract

When Mr Trump discussed the project with reporters in the Oval Office last month, he said the previous Biden administration had considered restoration options that would have cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

Mr Trump said he drew on his real estate experience and contacts to find a cheaper way.

"Over the years as a developer, I've probably built more than 100 swimming pools," Mr Trump said.

His past work gave him an idea, he said, which he took to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

"I said, 'You know Doug, I have a guy who's unbelievable at doing swimming pools' … I said, I have an idea, I'm going to send my contractor over to take a look.'

"He took a look at it, he called me up, he said, 'Sir, we can do something on it.'"

Loading...

Despite the anecdote, Mr Trump later claimed he did not know the contractor and had not used them before.

The denial came after the New York Times reported a "no-bid" contract was given to a company called Atlantic Industrial Coatings. The contract was awarded under an exemption meant for urgent situations to prevent "serious injury, financial or other, to the government".

Mr Trump responded to the report by attacking the Times and its "lowlife 'reporter'" in a Truth Social post.

"I didn't give out the contract, 'Interior' did, to a contractor I did not know, and have never used before," Mr Trump wrote.

Donald Trump shared this image on Truth Social as the project got underway. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

The cost

During his Oval Office press conference, Mr Trump said the project would cost "less than $2 million".

But the project contract actually turned out to be for $US6.9 million ($9.7 million).

And earlier this month, it was hiked up to $US13.1 million ($18.3 million).

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is the site of historic events like Martin Luther King's I Have a Dream speech in 1963. (AFP)

The New York Times, citing government documents, reported the new amount matched the figure that the contractor had quoted to do the job in March.

The Interior Department said the work needed to be fast-tracked for America's "250th birthday" celebrations on July 4.

The department told US media outlets: "The contract price reflects the effort necessary to expedite the timeline of completing the leak prevention coating project — more people, more materials, more equipment and longer hours ahead of our 250th."

The work is also supposed to repair some structural issues at the pool, which Mr Trump said was "in terrible shape".

"It leaked like a sieve," he said.

But some Americans see the change to the pool's colour as little more than a vanity project.

The United States Triumphal Arch, dubbed the "Arc de Trump", is another project planned by the president. (Instagram: Donald Trump)

"I think he should be focusing on other things," said Katie, the local student.

" We're at war in Iran right now, which most people can argue is not really necessary, and I think a lot of these more extreme things, like a ballroom, a big arch, it's more a distraction in my opinion and it's a waste of taxpayer money. "

"Trump has shown no respect for history," said Mike, the video producer.

World.title: As a child Rob was burnt. As an adult, he’s fighting fire with fire
World.content:
They huddled together under a woollen blanket on a country road, four children and a stalwart woman, desperately willing the raging bushfire to pass over them.

Moments earlier, they'd fled from the farmhouse in an FJ Holden ute as the fire swept across the property, setting the trees lining the driveway alight and sending flames leaping into the blackened sky.

Neighbour Dorothy Tucker was moving the children to safety … then the fire changed course. (Supplied)

As the children's neighbour and babysitter, Dorothy Tucker drove through the apocalyptic scene, a tree fell into the ute's path. It crashed.

Dorothy's only option was to bundle the kids, who she'd draped in wet towels, out of the ute and run for the road.

"That's when we all got burnt," Rob Armstrong, one of those children fleeing for their life that day, tells Australian Story.

"Running through the flames to get to the road because the flames were 30-foot high. It was just a ball of fire. I don't know how we lived."

Media reported the flames came within one metre of Dorothy Tucker's home and destroyed the shed. (Supplied: Ararat Advertiser, January 11, 1969)

Rob was just four when the fire tore through the hills near the Victorian town of Tatyoon In January 1969. His sisters Jen and Roz were eight and six and his brother Pete was only two years old.

The devastating bushfire made front page news. (Supplied: Ararat Advertiser, January 11, 1969.)

Rob knows two things saved them that day: Dorothy's bravery — and the arrival of farmers in their volunteer firefighting truck.

The farmers were heading toward the fire front, driving slowly as they navigated the thick, blinding smoke.

Suddenly, a man on the back of the truck yelled, "Stop!"

The smoke had cleared just a little, just at the right moment, for him to see the mound on the road.

"If he didn't yell out, the truck would have gone straight over the top of us," Rob says. "That's how close it was."

Jen, Pete, Rob and Roz were badly burnt in the fire, particularly on their feet and legs. (Supplied: Rob Armstrong)

Rob's admiration for volunteer firefighters with Victoria's Country Fire Authority (CFA) was forged that day.

"A volunteer firefighter [is] the guy that drops everything and goes and gets on a fire truck to try to save someone else's assets, their livelihood and hopefully save their lives, if they're in trouble."

Rob's been one now for 40 years. He has his own private fire truck ready to go at any time. He hates fighting fires — but he goes anyway.

What's happening? The Victorian government introduced the Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund (ESVF) to replace the existing fire services levy due to increased natural disasters.

Farmers face a threefold tax increase.

In late 2025 the government announced a two-year freeze for farmers at the lower 2024/25 rate.

In October 2025, the ABC reported Victoria's volunteer firefighter numbers had grown, despite fears farmers would quit en mass.

So, it felt deeply personal — and unjust — when the Victorian government announced in December 2024 that it would change the way fire levies were raised, ballooning the impost on many farmers. Big farms with significant improvements to the property faced an increase of up to 189 per cent.

At the time, Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan said the reason for expanding the existing levy to include all emergency services was to recognise the impact of all major weather events.

"[This] comes in recognition of the more frequent and fierce fire, flood and storm events that are impacting all corners of our state," she said at a press conference.

Rob described the increased taxes as "gut-wrenching".

“[The government] thought it would be a really good idea to increase the farmers’ levy by up to 189 per cent, which is probably the most gut-wrenching thing you could do to a farmer — especially when he’s the one that puts all the fires out,” Rob says.

“And I thought, ‘This is just not on. I’ve got to do something about this’.”

Volunteers jump on a truck on the Pyrenees Highway during the 1969 bushfire. (Supplied: Ararat Advertised, January 11, 1969)

Farming is 'bloody hard work'

Rob had a lot on his hands the day he got chatting to his neighbour down at the mailbox and learned about the proposed fire levy change.

At that time, his sheep property near Ararat had been in drought for a year — a drought that is still gripping much of Victoria and is considered by many farmers the worst since 1914.

“I was losing lambs that I shouldn’t have been losing because … the ewes only had dirt to eat except for the grain that I was supplying them,” Rob says.

" It is just soul-destroying. You have to be so strong just to keep going. Bloody hard work. "

Rob Armstrong is a sixth-generation farmer. (Australian Story)

Rob had also recently invested in another nearby farm, buying it in partnership with Sunny Berry, a family acquaintance who wanted to ditch her Melbourne corporate life.

When Sunny moved to the farm during COVID, she began tending to every orphaned lamb or injured kangaroo she found. It was not the type of farming Rob was used to.

“I think if I had a dollar for every time Rob said to me, ‘Oh, Sunny, no’, I would be a billionaire,” she says. “And I’d go, ‘Yes’, and then the animals would come back with us.”

Despite his reservations, Rob enjoyed seeing the animals recover and the happiness that tending to them brought Sunny.

Rob Armstrong runs about 526 hectares of wheat, barley and canola and 2,000 sheep. (Supplied: Rob Armstrong)

Over time, the duo became a couple.

“I think there’s a lot of things that make us an unlikely couple,” Sunny says. “There’s an age difference, a city-country person difference, but I think we’re both strange in our own way and in the same ways in some respects, which makes us totally perfect for each other.”

They now have a menagerie, from a male kangaroo called Karen that visits regularly and thinks it’s a cow, to a bunch of goats with their own Rob-built playground, a blind cow named Poppy, and Charlie, the cranky cockatoo.

Sunny moved from the city to the country and together the couple run the farm. (Australian Story: Simon Winter)

As Sunny settled into country life, she learned about the CFA and how “the people in those fire uniforms fighting the fires out here aren’t paid firemen".

"They’re farmers and local community people, mums and dads who do that on a volunteer basis," she says. “I think they’re incredible."

There are about 52,000 CFA volunteers. (Australian Story)

Sunny watched as Rob grappled with the Victorian government’s plans to change from an existing Fire Services Property Levy to an Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund (ESVF), which all ratepayers would pay. Calculations would vary depending on property type.

The ESVF would fund not just fire services, but a range of others, including Triple Zero Victoria and Victoria State Emergency Service. Similar schemes operate in most other states and the Victorian government argued the new levy was needed to ensure services were properly funded.

There was a concession to volunteer firefighters, with a rebate for properties valued less than $5 million.

But journalist Peter Hunt from rural newspaper The Weekly Times says many Victorian farms are worth between $10-$20 million.

The average farm’s levy would increase from $4,300 a year to about $12,500.

“It was a massive increase, pretty much a tripling of the amount farmers would have to pay and that’s why there was so much anger over it,” Hunt says.

The idea of farmers who risk their lives fighting fires being hit with such a hefty increase enraged Rob.

“You’re putting out the fire to save someone else’s assets and [they] expect us to pay for it? What’s right about that?”

Rob conducts a controlled burn on his property at Langi Logan, about 180 kilometres north-west of Melbourne. (Australian Story)

Rob decided to speak out, despite a strong aversion to the limelight. He contacted a bloke he knew who worked for Channel 10’s The Project and told his story.

He explained the vital role of volunteer firefighters, the effects of the drought and the importance of farmers to everyone’s food security. He warned farmers might stop volunteering to fight fires, becoming emotional as he said: “You feel like, why do we bother?”

Rob Armstrong says it was ingrained in him since birth to work hard on the land. (Supplied: Facebook/Rob Armstrong)

Simon Tol, a councillor with the nearby Pyrenees Shire, was watching that show. He contacted Rob and said: “What we should do is take a heap of fire trucks down to Melbourne and create a bit of exposure.”

CFA members converged on the Victorian parliament for a protest against the tax in May 2025. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

So that’s what they did. Peak hour traffic was brought to a crawl in Melbourne as trucks took over the streets and protesters chanted “scrap the tax”.

“It was absolutely frightening trying to organise about 40 or 50 fire trucks and a heap of utes,” Rob says. “It was a really daunting thing. But it was also a buzz.”

More rallies were held, each bigger than the last. Councillor Tol credits Rob with driving the protest movement. “He had microphone after microphone thrust in front of him,” he says. “Rob’s just become a media superstar.”

At least 20,000 people left their properties and headed to the city for the protest. (ABC News: Simon Winter)

Throughout it all, Rob stayed mute about what had happened to him and his siblings in 1969.

That wasn’t unusual. All the Armstrong kids had packed away that traumatic day – and the months they spent in hospital recovering from their burns — into the recesses of their minds.

Rob Armstrong wants to educate the public on the important role farmers play in the Australian economy. (ABC Archives)

But, as the rallies grew, Rob decided to tell their story even though “I find it really hard to talk about”.

In front of Victoria’s Parliament House, surrounded by signs reading “No farms, no food, no future”, Rob told the crowd about the day he almost died with his siblings and Dorothy.

And about how volunteer firefighting farmers saved them.

"There wasn't a dry eye in the area," Cr Tol says. "There was 20,000 people there … and you could have heard a pin drop in Melbourne."

Rob Armstrong has become an accidental leader in the fight for farmers. (Australian Story)

Two of those people were Jen Burrows and Pete Armstrong – Rob’s brother and sister.

“I just burst into tears,” Jen says. “And then after he’d finished his speech, we all just got together and had a bit of a hug. Really, we’d never talked about being burnt until that time.”

Angry farmers and CFA volunteers sent a clear message to the government about the proposed tax increase. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

By the end of last year, the Victorian Government bowed to the pressure, announcing the farm-value cap for rebates for CFA volunteers would increase from $5 million to $10 million, along with a postponement of the levy for all farmers for two years.

CFA chief officer Jason Heffernan says volunteer numbers are up after a "slight dip" during the protests and debate about the changes.

Rob says he’ll keep fighting the levy: “We’ve just won a fight but we haven’t won the war.”

But something else came from this accidental leader’s involvement in the protests – for the first time, the Armstrong siblings sat down and had a good talk about what happened to them that day in 1969.

After Rob's speech, he and his three siblings came together to talk through what happened to them in the bushfire for the first time. (Australian Story: Simon Winter)

Healing scars of the past

Over a cup of tea on a rambling verandah, fragments of memories bubble to the surface, each sibling sharing what they recall about their near-death experience and recovery.

Jen, Roz, Rob and Pete still bare scars on their feet from the bushfire. It's something they rarely speak about. (Australian Story: Simon Winter)

Roz Bowden remembers black skin hanging off their legs as they were ferried to hospital. Jen Burrows recalls the pain of burnt skin being scrubbed in a hydraulic bath. Rob pictures the plastic sandals they were wearing that melted and stuck to their feet as they got out of the crashed ute and took off for the road.

The burns to their feet were so bad, their soles have never grown back, causing ongoing pain. All up, the four children endured 40 operations.

“Why didn’t we talk about this as kids, or like as we’ve grown up?” Rob asks.

“Because,” says big sister Jen, “it’s such a fun topic!”

They all laugh. But, they reason, dissecting emotions and traumatic experiences is just not the country way, especially in that era.

“Keep a lid on it, just keep going forward and don’t look back,” Pete says.

Even the late Dorothy Tucker wanted to move on, rejecting any talk of an honour medal for her brave actions.

Mrs Tucker refused any honour for her role in saving the children from the fire. (Supplied)

But Rob is glad they're discussing that fire and its aftermath now.

"One thing I would like, if I get nothing else out of this, is that we learn to handle it better," Rob says.

“You’d think I’d start to get good at this and it wouldn’t upset me, but it just does.”

Fire trucks like this were used to fight bushfires across regional Victoria in January 1969. (Supplied: Facebook/CFA)

The more he thinks and talks about it, though, the more Rob understands what motivates him.

"If I look back at my life, being burned has definitely made me a volunteer," Rob says.

"But I think it's a lot deeper than that; that one day, I might save someone's life, like I was saved.

"I do think it's really created my drive, why I'm so against the emergency services levy they're trying to put on innocent people, people just like me, taking the risk out on their private units or in the CFA truck, trying to save someone's life."

The Victorian government did not take up Australian Story's offer of an interview.

Watch the Australian Story 'An Accidental Leader', Monday at 8:00pm (AEST) on ABCTV and ABC iview.

World.title: Sam Kerr ends glorious Chelsea career with record-equalling goal
World.content:
SportSoccerWomen's Super League Sam Kerr ends glorious Chelsea career with record-equalling goal Ian Chadband May 17, 2026 — 6:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sam Kerr has put a glorious seal on her pierless Chelsea career, scoring a virtuoso winning goal against Manchester United in her final match to leave as the club’s joint all-time top scorer. On an emotional day at Stamford Bridge – which had become “Samford Bridge” for one final Saturday – the Matildas skipper hammered home a fabulous volley in the 34th minute, her 116th goal for the club to match the all-time record of her former strike partner Fran Kirby. Loading She could even have broken the record, blazing one over in the 89th minute of Chelsea’s 1-0 Women’s Super League win, before coming off to a standing ovation all around the ground in stoppage time – even from United fans and players – as everyone saluted her 158th and final match for the Blues. View post on X



It was a fitting end to the 32-year-old’s stellar six-and-a-half year career for the London giants, having won five WSL titles, three FA Cups and three League Cups, as well as twice being crowned golden boot winner as the WSL top scorer. Sam Kerr celebrates her final goal for Chelsea – a glorious strike off a Lauren James assist. Getty Images Her English teammate Millie Bright, a 20-trophy veteran with Chelsea, was marking her farewell too, with the pair being given a guard of honour. “It was an amazing day, kind of fitting to play against Man United, a team I’ve scored so many of my favourite goals against, and to score one like that today was awesome,” said Kerr, who’s expected to announce she’ll be continuing her career in the NWSL in the US.



“It’s also fitting I end level with Fran after we played some pretty good football together. But I mean, every goal to me for this club is special, I enjoyed every minute today. “It’s just, honestly, the biggest honour to play for this club, and I have so many amazing memories which I’ll carry with me forever.” Kerr farewells Stamford Bridge. Getty Images She appeared with her one-year-old son Jagger in front of the cheering fans. “He’s born in Chelsea, so it’s kind of cute, and a nice little finish, but it was special to walk out with him and have my family here. A really sad day, but happy day, I guess,” she smiled. “It’s going to be hard to leave, but I’ve only good things to say about the club and the people here.”



Kerr then took the microphone. “Thank you to everyone who I’ve played with since I’ve been representing you guys,” she told them. “Week in, week out, every single minute for you guys. I’ve had some great personal memories both on and off the pitch, so thank you to all of you. Hopefully, you support me wherever I go.” View post on X Her send-off present to them, that instinctive and deadly first-time goal lashed in at the near post from a Lauren James cross, was enough to earn the victory that ensured Chelsea finished third in the table and sealed a place in the Champions League qualifiers next season. But the deposed champions finished behind Arsenal, who sealed second place with their 3-1 win at Liverpool, and champions Manchester City, who won 4-1 at West Ham, for whom another favourite Matilda, Katrina Gorry, played her final game.

World.title: Antoine Semenyo wondergoal wins FA Cup for Manchester City over Chelsea
World.content:
SportSoccerFA Cup Antoine Semenyo wondergoal wins FA Cup for Manchester City over Chelsea James Robson May 17, 2026 — 6:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Premier League with 4K on Stan Sport. Every match, live & on demand. Stream now

In its 155-year history, the FA Cup final can rarely have been won by a more audacious goal. Manchester City beat Chelsea 1-0 at Wembley Stadium on Saturday thanks to a moment of magic from Antoine Semenyo. The forward brought to life a final that had produced little in the way of chances or excitement with a spectacular back-heeled goal in the second half. FA Cup winners Manchester City. Getty Images Running onto a cross from Erling Haaland in the 72nd minute, Semenyo flicked his heel at the ball and directed it low into the far corner past diving Chelsea goalkeeper Robert Sanchez.



“It has happened a couple of times in training, it happened perfectly today. ... It came straight to me and I had to improvise myself as quickly as I can,” Semenyo told the BBC. “It is a good finish, I can’t lie.” Chelsea interim coach Calum McFarlane agreed. “For me, it’s a one in 100 goal,” he said. “For me, no, there’s not much more you can do to defend it.” Victory kept City in the hunt for a domestic trophy treble, having already won the English League Cup. Pep Guardiola’s team are also second in the Premier League, two points behind Arsenal with two rounds to go. With an important game against Bournemouth on Tuesday, Guardiola said he would not allow his players “even one beer” in celebration.



This was Guardiola’s 17th major trophy in 10 years at City and his 35th in his career overall. City have won the Cup eight times and moved level with Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham as equal third on the all-time winners’ list. Antoine Semenyo’s winning goal goes in. Getty Images Defeat means Chelsea will end the season trophyless – a year after being crowned Club World Cup champions – in what has been a crisis-ridden campaign. After firing two coaches since the turn of the year, Chelsea went into the final with a novice on the sideline in McFarlane, a former youth coach taking charge of only his seventh first-team game.



Related Article A-League Women Matilda’s heroics deliver Melbourne City A-League glory The turmoil at Chelsea led to supporters staging a protest against their American owners outside the stadium before kickoff. In that sense, it was commendable that McFarlane was able to frustrate Guardiola for such long periods. That was until Semenyo’s match-winning moment. The Ghana international joined City from Bournemouth only in January and made an immediate impact – scoring 10 goals and helping the team to two trophies.



“As a kid, I have always wanted to be playing for the top teams. It took a long time to get there, but I am grateful,” Semenyo said. “The first thing he (Guardiola) said to me when I came was, ‘Don’t change your game’ ... he still wants me to be me, still create a bit of chaos.” Loading After the final whistle, City fans sang the club anthem Blue Moon and cheered wildly as Bernardo Silva and John Stones lifted the famous trophy. Both players are leaving at the end of the season. “Being able to lift another trophy at Wembley, where we have played so many times, is such a special feeling, one I never take for granted,” Bernardo said. “To do so as captain makes this one of the best days of my career.”



Triumph for City came after back-to-back losses in the final in the previous two years. This was the record fourth year in a row they had reached the final, having last won it in 2023. Chelsea have lost their last four FA Cup finals, tying Leicester’s record for consecutive losses. Guardiola was congratulated by Prince William as he went to collect his winner’s medal. Afterwards the City manager gazed around Wembley at the celebrating fans. There has been growing speculation that this could be his final season at City; he has yet to confirm his plans. “The future is bright,” Guardiola said. “I know the guys, I know how they feel ... next year we will be there, we will be better next season.”
